## Changelog

Newest first. One line per change, with the reason when it isn't obvious. If you change a rule, log it here so nobody has to diff two versions of the guide to find out what moved.

## How to use this with an LLM

**1. Give it the whole guide.** Copy from the "Voice & Format Guide" heading down to the end. Don't cherry-pick sections — the rules reference each other, and the ones people skip (the proof points in §5, the house style in §2) are exactly the ones that keep output from sounding generic.

**2. Set it up once, not every time.** Paste it into a Claude Project, a ChatGPT project or custom GPT, or your tool's system prompt. Then it applies to every draft in that space and you only have to brief the task.

**3. Brief the task in one line.** Name the channel, the subject, and the client: _"LinkedIn post about the Axi rebrand."_ The guide already carries length, structure, and tone per channel. Naming the channel matters — a LinkedIn post and a tweet are different registers here, not long and short versions of the same thing.

**4. Never let it supply the numbers.** §5 is the only approved source for metrics, client outcomes, and proof points. If a draft contains a figure that isn't in §5, it's invented. Delete it or swap in a real one.

**5. Check three things before you ship.** Negative comparison (§2 — the most common failure by far), banned words (§2), and length against the channel spec (§3). Those three catch most of it.

**6. Give feedback by rule, not by vibe.** _"Rule 3 — the opener is a recap, not a position"_ gets you a fix. _"Make it punchier"_ gets you a reshuffle. The rules are numbered so you can point at them.

# Voice & Format Guide — Website, Blog Articles, LinkedIn, X

Properly is a design partner for modern finance — regulated brokers, DeFi protocols, neobanks. Finance is the only vertical this copy should sound like it's written for. Follow these rules for anything written on the website, in blog articles, or on social.

**Overall character:** we speak like a senior person who knows their subject deeply and doesn't need to prove it. Confident without being arrogant. Direct without being cold. Specific without being technical for its own sake.

**The positioning, in three lines:**

- **Why:** Modern finance is being rebuilt. Most companies building it look like they're not ready. We've designed for companies managing $15B in assets, and the ones that will.
- **How:** By treating every design decision as a trust decision, and knowing finance well enough to make the right one.
- **What:** We design financial products that earn trust and get remembered.

## 0. What we sell — and the approved copy for it

Four service lines, one expertise. **This is the canonical voice.** When you need to know how Properly sounds, read these before anything else in this guide — every other example is secondary to them.

**Homepage** — H1: _Design partner for the modern finance_ · H2: _From regulated brokers to protocols managing $15B. Eight years of financial design expertise._ · Section lead-in: _"Deep expertise. Four ways to apply it."_

**1. Branding** — H1: _Fintech branding agency_ · H2: _The identity that opens doors._ · Meta title: _Fintech Branding Agency | Properly Studio_

> Your brand is the decision made before you speak. Before your pitch starts, before your demo, before your product, investors, partners, and clients have already formed a view. Most of the time, it's based on what they saw. We design identities that make that first impression work for you, not against you, for fintech and financial services companies.

**2. Product Design (UX & UI)** — H1: _Fintech UX and UI design_ · H2: _Designing financial products._ · Meta title: _Fintech UX & UI Design Agency | Properly Studio_

> Your product works. It's time it looked like it. Every drop-off, every support ticket, every "I didn't understand that step" is revenue you're leaving on the table. In financial products, a confusing interface doesn't just cost you conversion, it costs you trust. We design products that users understand without a tutorial, and that your dev team can build without guessing.

**3. Website** — H1: _Fintech web design agency_ · H2: _Your website is your pitch._ · Meta title: _Fintech Web Design Agency | Properly Studio_

> Your website is your pitch before the pitch. A CMO, investor, or partner who lands on it has already formed an opinion before they read the first sentence. In financial services, that opinion is about trust. We build websites that close the conversation before it opens, because the right person lands, sees themselves in what's on the page, and reaches out, for fintech and financial services companies.

**4. Design Partner** — H1: _Your fintech design team. Without the hiring._ · H2: _For teams that want a partner, not a vendor._ · Meta title: _Hire a Fintech Design Team | Properly Studio_

> In the room when roadmaps are built. Not just when screens need designing. Design needs don't arrive in neat project shapes. One month it's a product feature. Next month it's a campaign. Then a new market entry, a pitch deck, a landing page that has to ship in a week. A Design Partner is a dedicated senior team that covers all of it, embedded in how you work, learning your brand and context once, and never starting over. Whatever you need, whenever you need it. Without the overhead of building a team to do it.

**Two more approved specimens** — the argument against generic AI-generated work, and the audit entry point:

> AI generates from what already exists. It has no point of view. No ability to say "this won't work." In a world of generated average, the most valuable thing a design studio can offer is conviction. Ours is built on eight years in finance.

> Most design studios spend the first month learning what a KYC flow is, why compliance disclaimers matter, and how your users think about money. We don't. That context is what allows us to make better decisions faster, and push back when something won't work.

## 1. The Five Rules

Test every sentence against this before it ships. Each rule has a wrong/right pair — match the right side, not just the principle.

**1. State, don't explain.** Every sentence says something concrete. Kill any sentence starting with "We believe" or "We feel," or any sentence that could sit on a competitor's site unchanged.

- Wrong: _"We believe that great design has the power to transform how financial products are perceived in the market."_
- Right: _"Finance is the only industry we design for. That changes everything."_

**2. Talk about the client, not yourself.** Most of the time "we" is the wrong subject — "your" is better. The reader should see themselves in the sentence.

- Wrong: _"We create brand identities that help financial companies grow."_
- Right: _"Your brand is the decision made before you speak."_

**3. Have an opinion.** Properly challenges briefs and pushes back — the copy should too. Name things. Take a position. Open with a stated position, not a neutral recap.

- Wrong: _"We take a collaborative approach to understanding your needs."_
- Right: _"Most rebrands solve the wrong problem. They make things look newer, not more credible."_

**4. Short sentences. Longer thoughts.** Sentence length signals confidence, not shallowness. A clear thought can stand alone in four words.

- Wrong: _"Our approach to financial design combines deep industry expertise with a rigorous creative process that ensures every deliverable is both aesthetically compelling and strategically sound."_
- Right: _"Finance is the only industry we design for. Eight years of it. Nothing gets approved without a reason."_

**5. Specific over general, always.** Numbers, names, moments beat adjectives. "$9.7B" beats "billions." "Axi" beats "a global broker." "Seven months" beats "quickly."

- Wrong: _"We've worked with some of the biggest names in crypto and fintech."_
- Right: _"We've designed for Axi, Sky, Spark, and NDAX. Together, their products manage over $15B in assets."_

## 2. Tone words & house style

**Use when accurate — don't force them:**

- _About the work:_ considered · precise · deliberate · rigorous · earned · enduring · intentional · distinct · specific · clear
- _About the relationship:_ partner · embedded · permanent · ongoing · accountable · challenged · pushed back
- _About the industry:_ trust · compliance · regulation · credibility · legibility · institutional · onchain · protocol · broker · regulated
- _About outcomes:_ opened doors · earned trust · built to last · designed to scale · made to be remembered

**Name the thing on the screen.** The tone words above are adjectives, and adjectives are the weakest sentence you can write about a product. When the subject is a product, reach for the interface object instead: order book, price level, order state, spread, fill, drop-off, disclosure, verification step. _"Every order state is visible before it's confirmed"_ carries more than any sentence about clarity, because the reader can picture it and a competitor can't copy it without having built the same thing.

**Banned — appear on every agency site, dead on arrival:**

passionate · innovative · world-class · holistic · seamless · pixel-perfect · leverage · empower · storytelling · transformative · cutting-edge · bespoke · tailor-made · elevate · solution · synergy · ecosystem (generic use) · exciting · proud to announce · thrilled · delighted

**Also avoid:**

- Passive voice: _"a rebrand was delivered"_ → _"we delivered a rebrand."_
- Vague time references: _"recently"_ → an actual date or timeframe.
- Unverifiable superlatives: _"the best," "the only," "the most"_ — unless it can be proven.
- Explaining what design is. The audience buys it; they don't need it defined.

**House style — mechanical rules, apply everywhere:**

- **Use contractions.** "It's," "wasn't," "we'd," "doesn't." Every channel, including the website.
- **Commas for pauses, not dashes for emphasis.** Dashes make copy feel breathless.
- **Avoid negative comparison. This is the single clearest tell of AI-written copy.** Defining something by what it isn't reads as machine-generated, and it's the pattern readers now spot instantly. It shows up in four shapes, all of them to be avoided:
    - _"It's not X, it's Y"_ / _"not X, but Y"_ — say what we ARE, positively. "We're a partner, not a vendor" → say what the partnership actually does.
    - _"It doesn't just X, it Y"_ / _"isn't just about X, it's about Y"_ — the most common LLM construction there is. Cut the setup and state the point.
    - **Back-to-back contrasts in the same paragraph.** Even one is fine occasionally. Two or three stacked is the tell.
    - **Short sentences that each negate the one before** — the trap Rule 4 sets. Tie the thought together with a connector (so, but, because, and) instead.
        - AI-sounding: _"The protocol worked. The interface didn't."_
        - Human: _"The protocol worked but the interface was built around protocol logic, not user intent."_
    - **The one allowance:** a single reversal, used as a closing line, where both halves are true. Anywhere else in the text, and stacked anywhere at all, it's the tell. **And the negated half has to be factually right** — a good reversal will happily carry a false claim past your ear. _"Volatility doesn't test your liquidity, it tests whether users can read the screen"_ reads well and is wrong, because volatility tests liquidity first. _"Volatility tests liquidity. It also tests whether your users can read the screen fast enough to act on it"_ keeps the turn and loses the falsehood.
- **Vary sentence length dramatically.** A 30-word sentence next to a 4-word one. Even rhythm reads as machine-written.
- **Don't describe AI in deficit terms.** When writing about AI tools, frame limits as where human craft still carries the work, not as the tool failing. Properly sells AI-adjacent design work and shouldn't sound like it's trash-talking the tools.
- **Capitalization:** always **Web3** (never "web3"). **DeFi**, **AI**, **TVL**, **KYC**, **NDAX** as shown — client names take the client's own casing, and NDAX is the one we keep getting wrong.
- **Terminology:** "design partners," not "agency" or "vendor," when describing the relationship. "Protocols," not "companies," for DeFi clients.

## 3. Format & length by channel

The words will keep evolving. These shapes and sizes are the stable part — hold new content to these counts unless there's a specific reason not to.

**The channel split, before the counts: social shows the product, articles show the process.** On LinkedIn and X, write the problem, the functionality that answers it, and what it costs the reader when it's missing. How we think, how the collaboration ran, how long we've been at it — that belongs in blog articles, where there's room to earn it. A post that spends its middle paragraph on our thinking has spent the space the product needed. Client tenure and team size are credentials, so they can appear as a half-clause, never as the subject of a sentence.

### Website copy

**The heading rule, before anything else: the H1 carries the search term, the H2 carries the slogan.** Everything below the H2 solves the reader's problem. This is a deliberate change. Headings used to carry slogans and almost no search terms, which left pages full of good copy with nothing telling Google or an LLM what they were about. LLMs cite pages whose headings name the thing, and a slogan gives them nothing to quote. The four service-line headings in §0 set the pattern for every page that follows.

|Element|Length|Notes|
|---|---|---|
|H1|3–7 words|The search term, plainly stated. Not a slogan.|
|H2|4–12 words|The slogan or positioning line that used to be the H1.|
|Body under the heading|45–90 words|A problem the reader recognises → what it's costing them → what we do about it.|
|Stat|1 number + 4–8 word label|Always in sets of 3.|
|Section intro|1–2 sentences, 15–30 words|Sits above a grid or list, sets up what follows.|
|Service/industry grid blurb|2–3 sentences, 30–45 words|One per card. Problem → what we do → outcome, in that order.|
|Package tier|Name + duration + 2–3 line scope|e.g. "Website — 21 days: Up to 10 subpages, Webflow, [outcome line]."|
|FAQ answer|60–160 words|State one position up front, then the breakdown.|
|Testimonial|30–70 words|One paragraph, always attributed: name, role, client.|

**For examples, use the four service lines in §0.** They are the approved new copy. The rest of the live site still runs on the previous positioning, so don't model new website copy on what's currently published there.

Testimonial that fits the new positioning (note the "willing to challenge" line, that's Rule 3 coming back as proof): _"It's extremely pleasant to work with Properly, the team is very knowledgeable, adaptable, and willing to challenge the management with convincing design decisions."_ — Bilal Hammoud, Founder & CEO, NDAX

### Blog articles

|Element|Length|Notes|
|---|---|---|
|Total body|850–1,600 words|Excludes SEO meta block.|
|Chapters|6–11 H2 sections (occasionally H3 sub-splits for paired comparisons, e.g. Lenders vs. Borrowers)|Many small chapters, not a handful of long ones.|
|Chapter length|60–300 words, most land 100–200|A chapter is one decision or one turning point, not a topic dump.|
|Chapter title|Names the decision or tension ("Naming as Product Design," "Two Vaults for Two Mindsets")|Never a generic label ("Overview," "Conclusion," "Introduction").|

Within each chapter:

- **Bold key terms** at the moment they're introduced (**Earn**, **Portfolio**, **Single Asset Vault**) — these are the words a reader would search for or repeat back.
- **Italicize real research quotes** as pull-quotes: _"What risk am I taking when I lend?"_ — never paraphrase into a generic pain point.
- Keep percentages and counts load-bearing throughout the prose, not parked in a stats callout: "roughly 70%," "around 30%."
- End each chapter on the decision or the result, not on process: "Naming is product design. Get the language right and half the confusion disappears before anyone touches the UI."
- Never over-explain basic design or DeFi concepts to a reader who already knows the space — cut definitional asides (rule 1).

**Example chapter, start to finish** (opening states a position, closing states the payoff — nothing in between explains what design is):

## The Starting Point: Too Much Data, Not Enough Guidance

DeFi apps don't have a data problem. They have a guidance problem. With too much information, you can't really tell what the most important metrics are, what the product's risks are, or how to pick the best yield for your needs.

With Silo, that meant rebuilding the whole thing from scratch, not just reskinning what was there. Here's how we did it.

Full copywriting mechanics beyond format (lead length, About-section rule of no numbers, one-paragraph-per-deliverable for case studies specifically) stay governed by the existing Case Study Guide — that one covers on-site case studies, this section covers blog articles.

### LinkedIn (Properly Studio company page)

Length is measured in **characters, not words** — finance vocabulary runs long (7+ characters per word is normal here), so a word count hides how heavy a post actually reads. A dense post can look mid-length by words and still be a wall.

|Element|Length|Notes|
|---|---|---|
|Reaction / testimonial|up to ~200 characters|Short, one thought.|
|Standard post|350–650 characters, 2–4 paragraphs|Case study, thought piece, partner content. Most posts live here.|
|Flagship|up to ~950 characters, up to 6 paragraphs|Multi-part recaps (e.g. three projects in one post). Only when the content earns the length.|
|Paragraphs|1–3 sentences each|Line breaks carry the pacing — no walls of text. Watch paragraph count before word count: 6+ blocks reads long even inside the character limit.|
|Hashtags|None|Instagram carries the hashtag load; LinkedIn company posts don't use them.|
|Emoji|0–1, only at the very end|🙏 🔽 👀 — never scattered through the body.|
|Link|Not in the post body|Close with "Full story in the comments," drop the link as the first comment manually after publishing.|
|Mentions|`@[Name](urn:li:organization:ID)`|Resolve new organizations via the Typefully LinkedIn resolver before tagging.|

Case-study, testimonial, process-recap, partner-content, and market-moment posts are the five recurring shapes — write in sentence case, full grammar, contractions ("it's," "wasn't," "we'd"). This is a different register from X (see below).

**Examples, one per shape.** These are published posts, so copy their _structure_ — but they were written under the previous positioning, so take the voice from §0 and §1, not from these. A post like the AI Hackathon one below opens with a neutral recap, which Rule 3 now rules out; under the new voice it would open with the position the hackathon proved.

- Case study reveal: "Everything here looks like one brand because there's one design system behind it. And that only happens with a longer collaboration. Trading, staking, quests, a leaderboard, an arcade mode, all @[Eterna Hybrid Exchange]."
- Testimonial: "A few genuinely kind words from the team on the Sentient rebrand. Grateful for the trust on this one, @[Sentient Foundation] 🙏"
- Process/result recap: "Here are the projects and results of our AI Hackathon: same brief, three completely different fintech apps, done by three different teams."
- Partner content: "Crypto's had a rough time living up to the word 'stable,' but lately the industry itself is starting to, less speculation, more plumbing: rails, accounts, settlement, compliance."

**The market-moment post has a fixed structure**, and it's the shape to reach for when something happening in the market gives a client feature a reason to be talked about today. Four beats: a market observation the reader already recognises → where that thing actually happens inside the product → the specific functionality that handles it → what volatility, or scale, or the moment in question really tests. Keep the client's name and category in the third beat, not the first, so the opening line earns the scroll on its own.

> When markets turn volatile, capital doesn't leave. It rotates into stablecoins, fast.

> That rotation happens inside the order book. Depth, spread and execution speed decide who protects their position and who doesn't.

> For @[NDAX], Canada's largest regulated crypto exchange, the Pro Trading interface is built for exactly this moment. Every price level stays legible at speed. Every order state is visible before it's confirmed.

> Volatility tests liquidity. It also tests whether your users can read the screen fast enough to act on it.

Eva Steen's LinkedIn (Nordic channel, separate account) keeps its own format — personal opener → cultural anchor → evidence → sharp idea → open question, 2–4 specific hashtags, no direct CTA — documented separately. Same Five Rules and tone words apply there; only the mechanics differ, because it's a personal-profile register, not the company page.

### X (contextual — will change fastest, don't over-index on it)

All-lowercase, fragment-driven register — a different voice from LinkedIn, not a shorter version of it. The casing and tone stay as-is; the subject matter is moving away from Web3/crypto and toward finance. Measured in characters like LinkedIn: ~100–280 per tweet (280 is the platform ceiling); threads run 5–10 tweets when going deep on one piece of work.

Example: "we ran an internal ai design hackathon at our studio, testing what ai can actually do for real client work. one brief (design a biometric fintech app), three teams, 14 hours. here's what came out of it 🔽"

A LinkedIn post rarely survives the trip to X intact — 280 characters usually forces you to drop one of the four market-moment beats. Drop the one about what the moment tests, keep the observation and the functionality: _"when markets turn volatile, capital doesn't leave, it rotates into stablecoins fast. that rotation happens inside the order book. @NDAXofficial Pro Trading keeps every price level legible at speed, and every order state visible before it's confirmed."_

### Dribbble

A separate register again, and the one people forget this guide doesn't cover. Shots open with a warm hook and an emoji, describe what's on the screen, carry a reusable "What is [Client]?" paragraph, and close with a live URL. Full mechanics, tag counts, and the authorship convention live in the Dribbble shot style guide — read that before writing a shot, and don't write one in the register of a service page.

## 4. Keywords

Search-demand data below is a snapshot, not a permanent fact — refresh periodically.

**The rule that shapes the whole list:** the US searches "fintech," the UK searches "financial services." Put the fintech term in the H1, the financial services term in the body. UK volume is smaller, but CPC runs $29–31 there — the highest-value buyers in the data — and UK organic is close to zero.

**Money terms (US), by target page:**

- Homepage / fintech hub: _fintech design agency_ (260–320/mo, difficulty 2 — the easiest real win in the cluster)
- Branding: _fintech branding agency_ (590/mo, difficulty 13 — the biggest commercial term, missing from the original list entirely)
- Product Design: _fintech ux design_ (260–390/mo)
- Website: _fintech web design_ (90–140/mo)
- Design Partner: _hire fintech designers_ (90/mo — thin, but the closest real term that exists)

**Money terms (UK):** _financial services website design_ (390/mo, the single largest term in the whole cluster, currently untargeted), _financial services web design_ (320), _financial services design agency_ (210), _fintech branding agency_ (90/mo, CPC $29.55).

**Content cluster (blog, informational):** _fintech logo design trends_ (480/mo), _fintech dashboard design patterns_ (390+/mo) — article topics, not page targets.

**Listicle intent:** "best fintech design agencies," "top fintech design agencies" — get into existing lists and publish our own. This is how Lazarev and Clay built their traffic, not through service pages.

**Defend — Web3 stays, as a layer under the finance story.** Every ranking Properly holds today is a crypto term rather than a fintech one: _web3 design studio_ (#1), _web3 design agency_ (position 23), _crypto design agency_ (25). That's the entire current organic footprint, so it doesn't get abandoned. **The split is roughly 80% modern finance, 20% Web3.** Treat this as an expansion of the story, not a pivot away from crypto — Web3 clients and Web3 language stay legitimate, they just stop being the headline.

**Drop — don't target these:** _defi design agency_ (zero volume), plus six phrases from the original keyword bank that don't appear in any real search data: _neobank brand identity agency_, _embedded design team finance_, _design partner for fintech_, _crypto exchange UI design_, _regulated broker rebranding_, _trading platform UX design_.

**Not keywords, but worth writing about:** MiCA, DORA, WCAG 2.2, RWA, KYC drop-off — strong article angles and credibility signals with zero measurable search volume. They live in §5 under Credibility topics. Use them to sound informed, not as page targets.

## 5. What you can reference — clients, proof points, topics

**In** — draw examples from these: Axi · Sky · Spark · Moto · Mento · NDAX · Sentient · Silo · Keel · Optio · Kado · RedStone · Quantstamp · Hydration · AngelBlock · Nomad Fulcrum

### Credibility topics

Trends the ICP is already thinking about. Referencing them earns credibility fast — they carry no search volume, so use them as article angles and supporting detail, not as page-targeting keywords.

- **Contextual finance** — cards and banking embedding into how people travel, work, and spend. The experience has to feel native to the context, not bolted on.
- **Fraud prevention as product experience** — communicating risk and guiding users through verification is a UX problem, not just a legal one.
- **Stablecoins as payment infrastructure** — flows and dashboards that work for crypto-native users and traditional finance operators at the same time.
- **ETF productisation** — ETFs packaged, branded, and distributed digitally as consumer products.
- **RWA tokenisation** — interfaces serving two audiences with very different trust expectations.
- **Wealth finance** — the unified dashboard for savings, investments, crypto, insurance, and spending.
- **Earned wage access** — trust is critical for users who are already financially stressed.
- **Regulation as a design constraint** — MiCA onboarding, DORA, WCAG 2.2 AA on trading interfaces, KYC drop-off, designing for compliance.

**Example article angles in this territory:** _"Why 60% of fintech users drop off during KYC, and what a better flow looks like"_ · _"What MiCA actually changes about onboarding design"_ · _"The problem with most financial rebrands (they solve the wrong problem)"_ · _"Why your design system is probably already obsolete"_

## 6. ICP framing cheat sheet

Ties the three counterparty profiles to how LinkedIn posts and articles should address each reader. Matches the existing 40/40/20 ICP weighting (Scaleups CMO / Scaleups Head of Product / Startup Founders).

|ICP|Say|Don't say|
|---|---|---|
|The Operator (CMO/Head of Marketing)|Lead with outcome, not process. Name the specific moment driving urgency (fundraise, competitor rebrand, launch). Talk about brand as a commercial tool.|"We're passionate about brand storytelling." "We'd love to learn more about your vision." Long process descriptions before relevance is established.|
|The Builder (CPO/Head of Product)|Diagnose, don't pitch — reference a specific product observation. Speak in design-system/dev-handoff/Figma-token terms. Lead with the audit as low-commitment entry point.|"We'd love to help you create an amazing user experience." Aesthetic-vision talk before metrics. Vague timelines.|
|The Founder (CEO/Co-founder)|Match their pace — direct, no preamble. Come in with a point of view, not a discovery questionnaire.|"Can you walk us through your vision?" Anything requiring them to do work before the engagement starts.|

This guide reflects Properly's current positioning and content roster as of July 2026 — revisit it as the roster and keyword data evolve.
